RESEARCH INFORMED CONSENT FORM FOR DEPARTMENT POOL PARTICIPANTS EARNING CREDIT IRB-FY2025-9903

STUDY TITLE: Narrative Comprehension IRB-FY2025-9903


INVESTIGATOR(S): David Poeppel, Hanzhi Chen


INVITATION TO BE A PART OF A RESEARCH STUDY:

You are invited to participate in a research study. This form has information to help you decide whether or not you wish to participate—please review it carefully. Your participation is voluntary. Please ask any questions you have about the study or about this form before deciding to participate.  


PURPOSE OF THE STUDY

The study is designed to learn more about how humans process and memorize narratives. In this study, we wanted to learn more about how people remember stories and decide whether certain details about them are true or false. Sometimes, when we remember things, we might recall them differently from what actually happened. We were interested in seeing how people agree or disagree on what they remember after hearing a story. 


DESCRIPTION OF STUDY PROCEDURES

If you agree to participate, you will be asked to listen to spoken stories. You will listen to a random set of two stories out of 4 existing options. After each story, you will see different statements about the story and decide whether you agreed with them or not, or sometimes multiple choice questions about details of the story. These statements were designed to test how well you remembered the story and whether your memory matched what other people remembered. The stories are each 8-13 minutes, and the questions should take 10-20 minutes for each story.

The research is being conducted by Prof. David Poeppel, Ph.D., who is the Principal Investigator, as part of his faculty research in the NYU Department of Psychology. If you agree to be in this study, you will be asked to: listen to auditory narratives that have been publicly recorded, make judgments to questions related to the content of the narratives.

RISKS OR DISCOMFORTS

There are no known risks associated with your participation in this research beyond those of everyday life. The data collected has the risk of a breach of confidentiality as they contain code associated in the SONA system with personal information.

BENEFITS

It is hoped that this study will contribute to your understanding of how knowledge is discovered in psychology and help the investigator better understand how memory of different events in a story is reflected in recall.

COMPENSATION

You will receive 1 credit. If you withdraw before the end of the study, you will receive credit for the time you have completed. If you choose not to participate, you can fulfill the course requirement in other ways besides participating in this study.

VOLUNTARY PARTICIPATION

Participating in this study is completely voluntary. You may choose not to take part in the study or to stop participating at any time, for any reason, without penalty or negative consequences. Not taking part or withdrawing from the study will not affect your grade or academic standing in any way. You have the right to skip or not answer any questions you prefer not to answer. When you complete the study, a thorough explanation of it will be provided.


If you withdraw from the study early but have already started on the survey questions, you will receive credit for the time you have completed. You should email the researcher with the number of questions you’ve completed.


If you withdraw or are withdrawn from the study early, then we will not keep information about you that is already collected.

PRIVACY & DATA CONFIDENTIALITY 

In this study, you may be asked to provide information that could be used to identify you personally. This information will be kept confidential. Only researchers and others that will keep the information confidential (e.g., regulatory agencies or oversight groups) may access information that could personally identify you. 

Confidentiality of your research records will be strictly maintained by assigning random code numbers to each participant and reporting all data in coded form. Your associated SONA ID will be kept in a secure location (NYU Box drive) separate from the data analysis. Your SONA ID is personally identifiable information as they can be connected to your name and email in the NYU SONA system. Information not containing identifiers may be used in future research or shared with other researchers without additional consent. The results of any portion of this study may be published in a book or journal or used for teaching purposes.

Information about you collected for this study may be shared with other researchers, used for other research studies, or placed in a data repository. These studies may be similar to this study or completely different. All information that could identify you will be removed before sharing the data or using it for other research studies. We will not ask you for additional permission before sharing the information.

The researcher cannot keep information confidential if they have concerns that someone is hurting children, that someone is hurting you, or that you might hurt yourself or someone else. In such cases, they will inform people in authority about their concerns. 

ACCESS TO YOUR STUDY INFORMATION 

We will not give you access to the information that is collected about you in this study. 


CONTACT INFORMATION

You are encouraged to ask questions at any time during this study. For information about the study, contact David Poeppel at (212) 992 7489 or david.poeppel@nyu.edu, 6 Washington Place, New York, NY 10003.  


If you have questions about your rights as a research participant or if you believe you have been harmed from the research, please contact the NYU Human Research Protection Program at (212)998-4808 or ask.humansubjects@nyu.edu.


AGREEMENT TO PARTICIPATE 

By continuing with this study, you agree to participate. Make sure you understand what the study involves before you agree. If you have questions about the study after you agree to participate, you should contact the research team. Do you wish to participate in the study?

Thank you for participating in our study. The aim of the study is to investigate errors in people’s memories. Imagine your friend is telling a story they heard – they might change or add details without realizing it. Here, you will be making judgments about whether a recollection of a story is accurate or not, given the original story.

This experiment consists of two sessions, each focusing on a different story.

In each session, you will first listen to the entire story. You will then be shown 30 sentences, which are recollections of specific parts of the story. Along with the context from the original story, you’ll see a rating given by another rater, indicating whether they believe the recollection is accurate or contains inaccuracies. The part identified to be inaccurate will be underlined.

Inaccuracies are parts of the recollection that either contradict the story or are not indicated by it. Your job is to decide whether you agree with the rater's judgment on whether the recollection is true (accurate) or inaccurate.

For each sentence, review the context and the rater’s assessment, then select "Yes" or "No" based on whether you think the rater's judgment is correct. In addition, rate your own confidence in this evaluation on a 1-5 scale.

The recollections are grouped such that every 5 recollections correspond to the same part of the original story. Remember to read the entire part of the original story before making your judgment.

Introduction

Introduction

You are invited to take part in a research study named Language comprehension: brain and behavioral mechanisms. The study is designed to learn more about how the brain processes language. If you agree to be in this study, you will be asked to: be interviewed about your handedness, and make judgments and responses to different types of auditory and visual stimuli, which may include sinusoidal or “pure” tones, noise, flashes, voices, speech and written words. Video/audio recordings may be taken to confirm that the tasks are performed correctly. You will be notified if these recordings will be taken. All personal identifying information will be removed from such recordings: the camera will be focused on your lips and hand(s), and these recordings will be assigned random codes for each participant for purposes of confidentiality.

Compensation

Your participation will take about 1 hour, and you will receive 1 credit. Risks and benefits

There are no known risks associated with your participation in this research beyond those of everyday life. Although you will receive no direct benefits for participation in this study, it may make you more aware of how knowledge is discovered in psychology and help the investigator better understand how the human brain interprets language.

Confidentiality

The code key connecting your name to specific information about you will be kept in a separate, secure location. Information not containing identifiers may be used in future research or shared with other researchers without additional consent. However, your name or other identifiers, such as voice or pictures that could identify you, will not be used in any publication or teaching materials without your specific permission, which will be requested in writing. No information that identifies you by name will be released without separate consent except as required by law. 

The researcher cannot keep information confidential if they have concerns that someone is hurting children, that someone is hurting you, or that you might hurt yourself or someone else. In such cases, they will inform people in authority about their concerns.

In accordance with the recommendations of the American Psychological Association, we will maintain study data for at least 5 years following publication in order to allow for potential replication and/or follow-up studies. data.word: This guy starts with talking about how he first got into his career in Journalism, and that was in college at Fordham University.
He recalls the place, but I don't quite remember it.
Rhode Island in Massachusetts? I forgot. Anyways.
He says that he was interviewing one of the deans because there was a dean who was trying to replace all the middle class working kids/students with more  kids, essentially.
So, the guy goes up to the dean ready for an interview, and it's like aren't you not be going back on this mission or aren't you not adhering to Fordham's Mission?
Just as the dean is about to answer, the guy sees a blur in the corner of his eye that gets bigger, and all of a sudden, this person throws a cream pie at the dean's face and then runs away.
The dean is now covered in cream.
They're both in shock, but the guy and the dean take a minute, and then the guy ask another question to the dean and says, “How do you respond to this attack?”
The dean - or do you have a response to the attack?
The dean says, “Yes, fuck you.”

So then, the guy rushes over to the editor-in-chief of the Ram, which is a newspaper on Fordham University's campus, and he goes to the editor-in-chief of who's this really big guy ends up winning the Pulitzer Prize, and he shows the editor-in-chief what he's got about the dean.
Then, the editor-in-chief says, “Yes, Dean, whomever, he's a dick.
Write that story up,” and so the guy gets really excited, and he goes and starts writing the story up.
It's his first-ever story.
He's really excited, and he writes a story up but better.
As in he ends up labeling the pie thrower, PM as Pie Man. Pie Man wears this cape.
Although, Pie Man didn't actually wear a cape.
He wears his cape.
I don't recall if they wore masks or not, but I do recall the cape.
Pie Man has a phrase in Latin, and even though it didn't make any sense, the author was Catholic.
So, Latin just came naturally to the author when making the catchphrase, and the catchphrase translated to “I am not a beast,” which is what Pie Man would say after an attack, or like for justice.
An attack for justice, not in a negative connotation.
That's how he wrote up the first story, and it got a lot of reads and was very popular.
In about 2 weeks later, the guy gets a letter from someone who says, I don't know, if you enjoyed my attack or I'm glad that you wrote about the story or something like that.
If you would like to see another event of Justice occur, please meet me at something library, like Myers Library steps at this time,” and signs it off as “from Pie Man.”
The guy ends up going to those library steps at that time and sees the student body president, who's female. I forgot her name.

She is, as the guy describes, well-bred and is not working class like most of the foreign student body was, and is wealthy and is basically the prime example of the kind of student the dean that had gotten his face covered in pie cream with wanted to replace the current board of students with.
Basically, he wanted more of student body, that student body president types rather than the current Fordham student body types.
She had worked together with the dean to create an alcohol ban because she thought that it was unbecoming to drink alcohol in public, on school campus.

The rumor is that she had also been very close with him in the office, like over the table, basically insinuating they had sex, but then the guy says, “Oh, but I would never spread that or I would never say that out loud.”
Then, he sees a blur and Pie Man is there again with his cape and his pie, and he throws it at the girl's face and runs away.
He says, “I'm not a beast” again in Latin.
At least that's how it's written in the newspaper, the way that the guy describes it as.

Now, at that point, it's kind of unclear whether - this is my side commentary, but now, it's unclear what actually really happened during the encounter and part of it was embellished, at least the first time around.
The new part was embellished.
The second time around, it's kind of hard to differentiate between what is real and what is embellished.
Anyway, back to the story.
The guy writes it up, the second encounter with the student body president. It's also a big hit.
There ends up being four or five stories or maybe it was four or five more stories about Pie Man, or maybe it was four or five stories in total about Pie Man throughout that entire year.
They were all written by the author and by the guy, the same guy. It's a big hit.

data.word: Okay, so the story began with a man - I don't remember his name but he was like - I don't know.

Basically, he found out that Dean McGowan of Fordham University was going to raise inflation on the students, and I don't remember how he met up with him but he found him and started ridiculing him or ask him why he was going to raise inflation.

He invented him, so he tells her yes, and that's all I remember.

Rhode Island in Massachusetts? I forgot. Anyways.

data.word: This guy starts with talking about how he first got into his career in Journalism, and that was in college at Fordham University.
He recalls the place, but I don't quite remember it.
Rhode Island in Massachusetts? I forgot. Anyways.
He says that he was interviewing one of the deans because there was a dean who was trying to replace all the middle class working kids/students with more  kids, essentially.
So, the guy goes up to the dean ready for an interview, and it's like aren't you not be going back on this mission or aren't you not adhering to Fordham's Mission?
Just as the dean is about to answer, the guy sees a blur in the corner of his eye that gets bigger, and all of a sudden, this person throws a cream pie at the dean's face and then runs away.
The dean is now covered in cream.
They're both in shock, but the guy and the dean take a minute, and then the guy ask another question to the dean and says, “How do you respond to this attack?”
The dean - or do you have a response to the attack?
The dean says, “Yes, fuck you.”

So then, the guy rushes over to the editor-in-chief of the Ram, which is a newspaper on Fordham University's campus, and he goes to the editor-in-chief of who's this really big guy ends up winning the Pulitzer Prize, and he shows the editor-in-chief what he's got about the dean.
Then, the editor-in-chief says, “Yes, Dean, whomever, he's a dick.
Write that story up,” and so the guy gets really excited, and he goes and starts writing the story up.
It's his first-ever story.
He's really excited, and he writes a story up but better.
As in he ends up labeling the pie thrower, PM as Pie Man. Pie Man wears this cape.
Although, Pie Man didn't actually wear a cape.
He wears his cape.
I don't recall if they wore masks or not, but I do recall the cape.
Pie Man has a phrase in Latin, and even though it didn't make any sense, the author was Catholic.
So, Latin just came naturally to the author when making the catchphrase, and the catchphrase translated to “I am not a beast,” which is what Pie Man would say after an attack, or like for justice.
An attack for justice, not in a negative connotation.
That's how he wrote up the first story, and it got a lot of reads and was very popular.
In about 2 weeks later, the guy gets a letter from someone who says, I don't know, if you enjoyed my attack or I'm glad that you wrote about the story or something like that.
If you would like to see another event of Justice occur, please meet me at something library, like Myers Library steps at this time,” and signs it off as “from Pie Man.”
The guy ends up going to those library steps at that time and sees the student body president, who's female. I forgot her name.

She is, as the guy describes, well-bred and is not working class like most of the foreign student body was, and is wealthy and is basically the prime example of the kind of student the dean that had gotten his face covered in pie cream with wanted to replace the current board of students with.
Basically, he wanted more of student body, that student body president types rather than the current Fordham student body types.
She had worked together with the dean to create an alcohol ban because she thought that it was unbecoming to drink alcohol in public, on school campus.

The rumor is that she had also been very close with him in the office, like over the table, basically insinuating they had sex, but then the guy says, “Oh, but I would never spread that or I would never say that out loud.”
Then, he sees a blur and Pie Man is there again with his cape and his pie, and he throws it at the girl's face and runs away.
He says, “I'm not a beast” again in Latin.
At least that's how it's written in the newspaper, the way that the guy describes it as.

Now, at that point, it's kind of unclear whether - this is my side commentary, but now, it's unclear what actually really happened during the encounter and part of it was embellished, at least the first time around.
The new part was embellished.
The second time around, it's kind of hard to differentiate between what is real and what is embellished.
Anyway, back to the story.
The guy writes it up, the second encounter with the student body president. It's also a big hit.
There ends up being four or five stories or maybe it was four or five more stories about Pie Man, or maybe it was four or five stories in total about Pie Man throughout that entire year.
They were all written by the author and by the guy, the same guy. It's a big hit.
Now, he's at a bar one day, at the end of the school year, I believe, and I know he's hanging out with some friends.
I know it was a bar and I know that there's this girl that he had been slightly flirting with, he says in a nuanced way.
So, nuanced back that like he doesn't think that she knows that he exists, and so he's just there and he's not talking to her.
Maybe she's with friends. All I know is that they're in a bar, for sure.

She ends up coming to him at some point and she says, “Hey, how have you been able to know - my friends and I were just talking about this, about how you have known where Pie Man is going to be for every attack before it happened,” and she says, “Are you Pie Man?”
That guy, at that moment, looks at that girl, and he knows he's not Pie Man, but he has a feeling, he knows that if he says yes, that he is Pie Man, that girl will have sex with him.
So, he does, I don't know, the logical thing or whatever.
He makes it seem essentially, when he describes the story, that he didn't say no, and then what comes out of his mouth is, weakly, “Yes, I am Pie Man.”
Then, the girl says, “Oh, tell me all about it -” no. “Buy me a drink and tell me all about it,” and that's how he ends.

data.word: This guy starts with talking about how he first got into his career in Journalism, and that was in college at Fordham University.
He recalls the place, but I don't quite remember it.
Rhode Island in Massachusetts? I forgot. Anyways.
He says that he was interviewing one of the deans because there was a dean who was trying to replace all the middle class working kids/students with more  kids, essentially.
So, the guy goes up to the dean ready for an interview, and it's like aren't you not be going back on this mission or aren't you not adhering to Fordham's Mission?
Just as the dean is about to answer, the guy sees a blur in the corner of his eye that gets bigger, and all of a sudden, this person throws a cream pie at the dean's face and then runs away.
The dean is now covered in cream.
They're both in shock, but the guy and the dean take a minute, and then the guy ask another question to the dean and says, “How do you respond to this attack?”
The dean - or do you have a response to the attack?
The dean says, “Yes, fuck you.”

So then, the guy rushes over to the editor-in-chief of the Ram, which is a newspaper on Fordham University's campus, and he goes to the editor-in-chief of who's this really big guy ends up winning the Pulitzer Prize, and he shows the editor-in-chief what he's got about the dean.
Then, the editor-in-chief says, “Yes, Dean, whomever, he's a dick.
Write that story up,” and so the guy gets really excited, and he goes and starts writing the story up.
It's his first-ever story.
He's really excited, and he writes a story up but better.
As in he ends up labeling the pie thrower, PM as Pie Man. Pie Man wears this cape.
Although, Pie Man didn't actually wear a cape.
He wears his cape.
I don't recall if they wore masks or not, but I do recall the cape.
Pie Man has a phrase in Latin, and even though it didn't make any sense, the author was Catholic.
So, Latin just came naturally to the author when making the catchphrase, and the catchphrase translated to “I am not a beast,” which is what Pie Man would say after an attack, or like for justice.
An attack for justice, not in a negative connotation.
That's how he wrote up the first story, and it got a lot of reads and was very popular.
In about 2 weeks later, the guy gets a letter from someone who says, I don't know, if you enjoyed my attack or I'm glad that you wrote about the story or something like that.
If you would like to see another event of Justice occur, please meet me at something library, like Myers Library steps at this time,” and signs it off as “from Pie Man.”
The guy ends up going to those library steps at that time and sees the student body president, who's female. I forgot her name.

She is, as the guy describes, well-bred and is not working class like most of the foreign student body was, and is wealthy and is basically the prime example of the kind of student the dean that had gotten his face covered in pie cream with wanted to replace the current board of students with.
Basically, he wanted more of student body, that student body president types rather than the current Fordham student body types.
She had worked together with the dean to create an alcohol ban because she thought that it was unbecoming to drink alcohol in public, on school campus.

The rumor is that she had also been very close with him in the office, like over the table, basically insinuating they had sex, but then the guy says, “Oh, but I would never spread that or I would never say that out loud.”
Then, he sees a blur and Pie Man is there again with his cape and his pie, and he throws it at the girl's face and runs away.
He says, “I'm not a beast” again in Latin.
At least that's how it's written in the newspaper, the way that the guy describes it as.

Now, at that point, it's kind of unclear whether - this is my side commentary, but now, it's unclear what actually really happened during the encounter and part of it was embellished, at least the first time around.
The new part was embellished.
The second time around, it's kind of hard to differentiate between what is real and what is embellished.
Anyway, back to the story.
The guy writes it up, the second encounter with the student body president. It's also a big hit.
There ends up being four or five stories or maybe it was four or five more stories about Pie Man, or maybe it was four or five stories in total about Pie Man throughout that entire year.
They were all written by the author and by the guy, the same guy. It's a big hit.
Now, he's at a bar one day, at the end of the school year, I believe, and I know he's hanging out with some friends.
I know it was a bar and I know that there's this girl that he had been slightly flirting with, he says in a nuanced way.
So, nuanced back that like he doesn't think that she knows that he exists, and so he's just there and he's not talking to her.
Maybe she's with friends. All I know is that they're in a bar, for sure.

She ends up coming to him at some point and she says, “Hey, how have you been able to know - my friends and I were just talking about this, about how you have known where Pie Man is going to be for every attack before it happened,” and she says, “Are you Pie Man?”
That guy, at that moment, looks at that girl, and he knows he's not Pie Man, but he has a feeling, he knows that if he says yes, that he is Pie Man, that girl will have sex with him.
So, he does, I don't know, the logical thing or whatever.
He makes it seem essentially, when he describes the story, that he didn't say no, and then what comes out of his mouth is, weakly, “Yes, I am Pie Man.”
Then, the girl says, “Oh, tell me all about it -” no. “Buy me a drink and tell me all about it,” and that's how he ends.

data.word: Okay, so the story began with a man - I don't remember his name but he was like - I don't know.

Basically, he found out that Dean McGowan of Fordham University was going to raise inflation on the students, and I don't remember how he met up with him but he found him and started ridiculing him or ask him why he was going to raise inflation.
Then this man apparently appeared with the cream pie and shoved it in Dean McGowan’s face and then ran away.
Then the speaker asked the dean how he felt about it and he said, “F you.”

Then the guy proceeds to go home and he says to himself that it's a good story but it needs embellishing, so he goes home and he writes about the encounter with the dean and the guy who threw the cream pie, but he changes the story by saying the guy who threw the cream pie was now a superhero named Pie Man, PM for short.
He said a Latin catchphrase like “I am not an animal” or something like that.
Then he said that he wore a cape and stuff, and then he took the story - I guess he’s an editor for a newspaper or something, and then he took the story to his chief editor, something like that.
He says, “Wow, this is a great story. I’m printing it on page one.”
Then his story comes out and I guess everybody likes it.
Then he met with someone at a hotel, I don't remember much about that part of the story, like a childhood friend or something.
I don't remember that part, but then he writes I think five more stories or he continues to write them.
Then he goes to a bar one night and meets a girl named Amanda I believe, and he has a crush on her or he says like they were flirting, but then he said he was actually the only one flirting with her.
She says, “It’s really strange how you know where Pie Man is at all times. Are you Pie Man?”
He goes, “If I say yes, she'll have sex with me,” so he tells himself he basically is Pie Man because he created him.
He invented him, so he tells her yes, and that's all I remember.

data.word: This guy starts with talking about how he first got into his career in Journalism, and that was in college at Fordham University.
He recalls the place, but I don't quite remember it.
Rhode Island in Massachusetts? I forgot. Anyways.
He says that he was interviewing one of the deans because there was a dean who was trying to replace all the middle class working kids/students with more  kids, essentially.
So, the guy goes up to the dean ready for an interview, and it's like aren't you not be going back on this mission or aren't you not adhering to Fordham's Mission?
Just as the dean is about to answer, the guy sees a blur in the corner of his eye that gets bigger, and all of a sudden, this person throws a cream pie at the dean's face and then runs away.
The dean is now covered in cream.
They're both in shock, but the guy and the dean take a minute, and then the guy ask another question to the dean and says, “How do you respond to this attack?”
The dean - or do you have a response to the attack?
The dean says, “Yes, fuck you.”

So then, the guy rushes over to the editor-in-chief of the Ram, which is a newspaper on Fordham University's campus, and he goes to the editor-in-chief of who's this really big guy ends up winning the Pulitzer Prize, and he shows the editor-in-chief what he's got about the dean.
Then, the editor-in-chief says, “Yes, Dean, whomever, he's a dick.
Write that story up,” and so the guy gets really excited, and he goes and starts writing the story up.
It's his first-ever story.
He's really excited, and he writes a story up but better.
As in he ends up labeling the pie thrower, PM as Pie Man. Pie Man wears this cape.
Although, Pie Man didn't actually wear a cape.
He wears his cape.
I don't recall if they wore masks or not, but I do recall the cape.
Pie Man has a phrase in Latin, and even though it didn't make any sense, the author was Catholic.
So, Latin just came naturally to the author when making the catchphrase, and the catchphrase translated to “I am not a beast,” which is what Pie Man would say after an attack, or like for justice.
An attack for justice, not in a negative connotation.
That's how he wrote up the first story, and it got a lot of reads and was very popular.
In about 2 weeks later, the guy gets a letter from someone who says, I don't know, if you enjoyed my attack or I'm glad that you wrote about the story or something like that.
If you would like to see another event of Justice occur, please meet me at something library, like Myers Library steps at this time,” and signs it off as “from Pie Man.”
The guy ends up going to those library steps at that time and sees the student body president, who's female. I forgot her name.

She is, as the guy describes, well-bred and is not working class like most of the foreign student body was, and is wealthy and is basically the prime example of the kind of student the dean that had gotten his face covered in pie cream with wanted to replace the current board of students with.
Basically, he wanted more of student body, that student body president types rather than the current Fordham student body types.
She had worked together with the dean to create an alcohol ban because she thought that it was unbecoming to drink alcohol in public, on school campus.

The rumor is that she had also been very close with him in the office, like over the table, basically insinuating they had sex, but then the guy says, “Oh, but I would never spread that or I would never say that out loud.”
Then, he sees a blur and Pie Man is there again with his cape and his pie, and he throws it at the girl's face and runs away.
He says, “I'm not a beast” again in Latin.
At least that's how it's written in the newspaper, the way that the guy describes it as.

Now, at that point, it's kind of unclear whether - this is my side commentary, but now, it's unclear what actually really happened during the encounter and part of it was embellished, at least the first time around.
The new part was embellished.
The second time around, it's kind of hard to differentiate between what is real and what is embellished.
Anyway, back to the story.
The guy writes it up, the second encounter with the student body president. It's also a big hit.
There ends up being four or five stories or maybe it was four or five more stories about Pie Man, or maybe it was four or five stories in total about Pie Man throughout that entire year.
They were all written by the author and by the guy, the same guy. It's a big hit.
Now, he's at a bar one day, at the end of the school year, I believe, and I know he's hanging out with some friends.
I know it was a bar and I know that there's this girl that he had been slightly flirting with, he says in a nuanced way.
So, nuanced back that like he doesn't think that she knows that he exists, and so he's just there and he's not talking to her.
Maybe she's with friends. All I know is that they're in a bar, for sure.

She ends up coming to him at some point and she says, “Hey, how have you been able to know - my friends and I were just talking about this, about how you have known where Pie Man is going to be for every attack before it happened,” and she says, “Are you Pie Man?”
That guy, at that moment, looks at that girl, and he knows he's not Pie Man, but he has a feeling, he knows that if he says yes, that he is Pie Man, that girl will have sex with him.
So, he does, I don't know, the logical thing or whatever.
He makes it seem essentially, when he describes the story, that he didn't say no, and then what comes out of his mouth is, weakly, “Yes, I am Pie Man.”
Then, the girl says, “Oh, tell me all about it -” no. “Buy me a drink and tell me all about it,” and that's how he ends.

data.word: okay. So, basically what happened in this story was that this journalist at Fordham University, first of all, was hating on it, number one; number two, he was walking on campus and he saw the dean of the campus, so he decided to ask him questions.
He asked him, is it true that he is raising the tuition, so there's more, you know, well-bred, I guess, and wealthy students coming to Fordham rather than middle-class students.

And he decided to answer that question by saying, “Listen here, you punk…” - but next thing you know it, there's another person next to the journalist coming out of nowhere and slamming pie in the dean's face.
The journalist then is shocked and - but he continues to ask the dean, “Would  you like to say anything else about the incident that just happened?”
And then the dean said something - I don't know what he said.

But instead, the journalist decides to go back to his editor because he was like, “You know what, this is a great scoop. This is amazing. No, I don't like the dean, so I'm just going to go to my editor.”
His editor is a pretty big man.
He goes to his editor and tells him what happened, and the editor is just like, “You know what, yeah, that guy's a dick. Yeah, go ahead and do it.“
So, he decides to write his story upon the man who slammed pie at Dean McGallagher’s face.
So, he writes the story, but he goes above and beyond with it.
I mean, he goes to the boundary by adding shit that didn't even happen.
So, he decides to portray Pie Man as if it was this Marvel superhero by adding a cape, calling him capital PM, like everything.
And the villain, of course, would be the dean.

He talks about how this Pie Man, he saves - he attacks - not attacks, but he slams pie at people who deserve it, such as the dean, and he has specific catchphrase that's in Latin, but I don't remember what it was in Latin, but it was something like “I am the monster” or something, that's has to do with that.
But the journalist said that it has completely nothing to do with the Pie Man, rather, it was just something he remembered, like from Latin, he just remembered that.
So, he was like, you know what, let me just use Latin in this.
So, he makes the story, he shows his friend, and his friend is - not friend, his editor.
He tells his editor, and his editor is just like, “You know what, this is great, this is good. Let's do it, let's publish this.”

So, it becomes published and, you know, nothing really much happens until a couple of days later, he gets something in the mail, and the mail is from Pie Man, stating how he should be at the steps, at the door steps of Dean McGallagher’s at 3:00 PM.
So, he goes there, but on his way there, he sees this girl saying - I don't know her name, but this girl, she’s specifically one of the students Dean McGallagher likes.
I mean, well bred, has a bunch of school spirit, and then the journalist made a joke about how there's a bunch of those girls in his desk, but - it was a joke, he said it was a rumor.
But anyways, going back to the story.
He goes on to explain, she's the girl that got drinking outside bands, like - I mean, like drinking at a barbecue band, so you know, people don't really like her.
But when he goes by her, out of nowhere, PM comes at a nowhere, and smacks pie in that girl's face.

So, she's just like - so obviously, the journalist was just like, “What just happened?” and then the Pie Man apparently finds out - well, he finds out that the Pie Man left saying Latin, but - it didn't actually happen, that catchphrase in Latin was in the newspapers, like every single newspaper out there, I mean, multiple sources off the campus one.
So, that happens, and a couple of days later - I mean, not a couple of days later, but it goes so far, and he sees this girl in his class that he's been flirting with for a while.

Well, they've been going back and forth for two months, that's what he thought, but more so he comes to find out that it's more just him flirting with her, and he's just like - he thinks that she doesn't remember her, so - he thinks that she doesn’t remember him, so he's just moving on, you know, just doing what he has to do, until he feels a tap on his shoulder, and he turns around, it's the same girl.

Like, he's always around Pie Man; wherever Pie Man is, he's there.

So, she proceeds to ask him if he was Pie Man, Now, he thought about this, the journalist thought about it, he was like, “You know what, I can take his opportunity to bring this girl if I say yes, but that'd be a lie, but you know what, I think it's worth it.”
But eventually, he was just like, “No, I'm not P-Man.” I mean, no, he said yes, that he is P-Man. Even though he didn't think about the consequences, he said yes, that he is P-Man, and – yes.

data.word: This guy starts with talking about how he first got into his career in Journalism, and that was in college at Fordham University.
He recalls the place, but I don't quite remember it.
Rhode Island in Massachusetts? I forgot. Anyways.
He says that he was interviewing one of the deans because there was a dean who was trying to replace all the middle class working kids/students with more  kids, essentially.
So, the guy goes up to the dean ready for an interview, and it's like aren't you not be going back on this mission or aren't you not adhering to Fordham's Mission?
Just as the dean is about to answer, the guy sees a blur in the corner of his eye that gets bigger, and all of a sudden, this person throws a cream pie at the dean's face and then runs away.
The dean is now covered in cream.
They're both in shock, but the guy and the dean take a minute, and then the guy ask another question to the dean and says, “How do you respond to this attack?”
The dean - or do you have a response to the attack?
The dean says, “Yes, fuck you.”

So then, the guy rushes over to the editor-in-chief of the Ram, which is a newspaper on Fordham University's campus, and he goes to the editor-in-chief of who's this really big guy ends up winning the Pulitzer Prize, and he shows the editor-in-chief what he's got about the dean.
Then, the editor-in-chief says, “Yes, Dean, whomever, he's a dick.
Write that story up,” and so the guy gets really excited, and he goes and starts writing the story up.
It's his first-ever story.
He's really excited, and he writes a story up but better.
As in he ends up labeling the pie thrower, PM as Pie Man. Pie Man wears this cape.
Although, Pie Man didn't actually wear a cape.
He wears his cape.
I don't recall if they wore masks or not, but I do recall the cape.
Pie Man has a phrase in Latin, and even though it didn't make any sense, the author was Catholic.
So, Latin just came naturally to the author when making the catchphrase, and the catchphrase translated to “I am not a beast,” which is what Pie Man would say after an attack, or like for justice.
An attack for justice, not in a negative connotation.
That's how he wrote up the first story, and it got a lot of reads and was very popular.
In about 2 weeks later, the guy gets a letter from someone who says, I don't know, if you enjoyed my attack or I'm glad that you wrote about the story or something like that.
If you would like to see another event of Justice occur, please meet me at something library, like Myers Library steps at this time,” and signs it off as “from Pie Man.”
The guy ends up going to those library steps at that time and sees the student body president, who's female. I forgot her name.

She is, as the guy describes, well-bred and is not working class like most of the foreign student body was, and is wealthy and is basically the prime example of the kind of student the dean that had gotten his face covered in pie cream with wanted to replace the current board of students with.
Basically, he wanted more of student body, that student body president types rather than the current Fordham student body types.
She had worked together with the dean to create an alcohol ban because she thought that it was unbecoming to drink alcohol in public, on school campus.

The rumor is that she had also been very close with him in the office, like over the table, basically insinuating they had sex, but then the guy says, “Oh, but I would never spread that or I would never say that out loud.”
Then, he sees a blur and Pie Man is there again with his cape and his pie, and he throws it at the girl's face and runs away.
He says, “I'm not a beast” again in Latin.
At least that's how it's written in the newspaper, the way that the guy describes it as.

Now, at that point, it's kind of unclear whether - this is my side commentary, but now, it's unclear what actually really happened during the encounter and part of it was embellished, at least the first time around.
The new part was embellished.
The second time around, it's kind of hard to differentiate between what is real and what is embellished.
Anyway, back to the story.
The guy writes it up, the second encounter with the student body president. It's also a big hit.
There ends up being four or five stories or maybe it was four or five more stories about Pie Man, or maybe it was four or five stories in total about Pie Man throughout that entire year.
They were all written by the author and by the guy, the same guy. It's a big hit.
Now, he's at a bar one day, at the end of the school year, I believe, and I know he's hanging out with some friends.
I know it was a bar and I know that there's this girl that he had been slightly flirting with, he says in a nuanced way.
So, nuanced back that like he doesn't think that she knows that he exists, and so he's just there and he's not talking to her.
Maybe she's with friends. All I know is that they're in a bar, for sure.

She ends up coming to him at some point and she says, “Hey, how have you been able to know - my friends and I were just talking about this, about how you have known where Pie Man is going to be for every attack before it happened,” and she says, “Are you Pie Man?”
That guy, at that moment, looks at that girl, and he knows he's not Pie Man, but he has a feeling, he knows that if he says yes, that he is Pie Man, that girl will have sex with him.
So, he does, I don't know, the logical thing or whatever.
He makes it seem essentially, when he describes the story, that he didn't say no, and then what comes out of his mouth is, weakly, “Yes, I am Pie Man.”
Then, the girl says, “Oh, tell me all about it -” no. “Buy me a drink and tell me all about it,” and that's how he ends.

He asked him, is it true that he is raising the tuition, so there's more, you know, well-bred, I guess, and wealthy students coming to Fordham rather than middle-class students.

And he decided to answer that question by saying, “Listen here, you punk…” - but next thing you know it, there's another person next to the journalist coming out of nowhere and slamming pie in the dean's face.
The journalist then is shocked and - but he continues to ask the dean, “Would  you like to say anything else about the incident that just happened?”
And then the dean said something - I don't know what he said.

His editor is a pretty big man.

INVITATION TO BE A PART OF A RESEARCH STUDY:

You are invited to participate in a research study. This form has information to help you decide whether or not you wish to participate—please review it carefully. Your participation is voluntary. Please ask any questions you have about the study or about this form before deciding to participate.  


PURPOSE OF THE STUDY

The study is designed to learn more about how humans process and memorize narratives. In this study, we wanted to learn more about how people remember stories and decide whether certain details about them are true or false. Sometimes, when we remember things, we might recall them differently from what actually happened. We were interested in seeing how people agree or disagree on what they remember after hearing a story. 


DESCRIPTION OF STUDY PROCEDURES

If you agree to participate, you will be asked to listen to spoken stories. You will listen to a random set of two stories out of 4 existing options. PURPOSE OF THE STUDY

The study is designed to learn more about how humans process and memorize narratives. In this study, we wanted to learn more about how people remember stories and decide whether certain details about them are true or false. Sometimes, when we remember things, we might recall them differently from what actually happened. We were interested in seeing how people agree or disagree on what they remember after hearing a story. 


DESCRIPTION OF STUDY PROCEDURES

If you agree to participate, you will be asked to listen to spoken stories. You will listen to a random set of two stories out of 4 existing options. These statements were designed to test how well you remembered the story and whether your memory matched what other people remembered. The stories are each 8-13 minutes, and the questions should take 10-20 minutes for each story.

These statements were designed to test how well you remembered the story and whether your memory matched what other people remembered. Thank you for participating in our study. The aim of the study is to investigate errors in people’s memories. Imagine your friend is telling a story they heard – they might change or add details without realizing it. Here, you will be making judgments about whether a recollection of a story is accurate or not, given the original story.

This experiment consists of two sessions, each focusing on a different story.

In each session, you will first listen to the entire story. You will then be shown 30 sentences, which are recollections of specific parts of the story. Along with the context from the original story, you’ll see a rating given by another rater, indicating whether they believe the recollection is accurate or contains inaccuracies. The part identified to be inaccurate will be underlined.

PURPOSE OF THE STUDY

The study is designed to learn more about how humans process and memorize narratives. In this study, we wanted to learn more about how people remember stories and decide whether certain details about them are true or false. Sometimes, when we remember things, we might recall them differently from what actually happened. We were interested in seeing how people agree or disagree on what they remember after hearing a story. 


DESCRIPTION OF STUDY PROCEDURES

If you agree to participate, you will be asked to listen to spoken stories. You will listen to a random set of two stories out of 4 existing options. After each story, you will see different statements about the story and decide whether you agreed with them or not, or sometimes multiple choice questions about details of the story. These statements were designed to test how well you remembered the story and whether your memory matched what other people remembered. The stories are each 8-13 minutes, and the questions should take 10-20 minutes for each story.

The research is being conducted by Prof. David Poeppel, Ph.D., who is the Principal Investigator, as part of his faculty research in the NYU Department of Psychology. If you agree to be in this study, you will be asked to: listen to auditory narratives that have been publicly recorded, make judgments to questions related to the content of the narratives.

Thank you for participating in our study. The aim of the study is to investigate errors in people’s memories. Imagine your friend is telling a story they heard – they might change or add details without realizing it. Here, you will be making judgments about whether a recollection of a story is accurate or not, given the original story.

This experiment consists of two sessions, each focusing on a different story.

In each session, you will first listen to the entire story. You will then be shown 30 sentences, which are recollections of specific parts of the story. Along with the context from the original story, you’ll see a rating given by another rater, indicating whether they believe the recollection is accurate or contains inaccuracies. The part identified to be inaccurate will be underlined.

Inaccuracies are parts of the recollection that either contradict the story or are not indicated by it. Your job is to decide whether you agree with the rater's judgment on whether the recollection is true (accurate) or inaccurate.

For each sentence, review the context and the rater’s assessment, then select "Yes" or "No" based on whether you think the rater's judgment is correct. In addition, rate your own confidence in this evaluation on a 1-5 scale.

The study is designed to learn more about how humans process and memorize narratives.
